stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of multiple colonic diverticula presents with massive, painless hematochezia. Colonoscopy reveals diverticula throughout the colon, but none are actively bleeding at the time of examination. What is the most likely source of bleeding?
expl: Diverticula form where the vasa recta penetrate the colonic wall; the vessel stretched over the dome ruptures → painless massive bleeding, often stopped by the time of colonoscopy.

why.A: Cancer causes slow, occult or mixed bleeding.
why.C: Haemorrhoids give bright red bleeding on the paper, not massive haematochezia.
why.D: Angiodysplasia is possible, but with diverticula throughout and massive painless bleeding the vasa recta are the classic source.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with IBD (mild colitis on colonoscopy a year ago) presents with haematochezia. What is the cause?
ansText: Most likely a flare of her inflammatory bowel disease (the recall gave "Crohn's flare / CRC") — long-standing colitis also raises colorectal cancer risk, so colonoscopy is needed.

stem: A 20-year-old man, otherwise healthy, presented to the outpatient department complaining of per-rectal bleeding for 3 months. Anorectal examination showed 3rd degree hemorrhoids. He has a family history of Colon cancer and Symptoms of Iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in management?
expl: Rectal bleeding with iron-deficiency anaemia and a family history of colon cancer → colonoscopy to exclude a proximal lesion before attributing bleeding to haemorrhoids.

why.A: Treating the haemorrhoids first could miss cancer.
why.B: Treating the haemorrhoids first could miss cancer.
why.C: Upper endoscopy isn't first for fresh rectal bleeding.

stem: 28 Y/O male presented with 10-15 episodes of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. He was treated as a case of acute gastroenteritis but the bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain did not improve. During examination he looks dehydrated with low blood pressure and cachectic. What is the initial management t?

opts.t: Refer him and continue treatment as gastroenteritis
Admit and rehydrate him with IV fluid

expl: Severe bloody diarrhoea not responding to gastroenteritis treatment, dehydrated, hypotensive, cachectic → admit and resuscitate with IV fluids first, then investigate (acute severe colitis).

why.C: Too sick for outpatient work-up.
why.D: OR only for complications (perforation, toxic megacolon, failure of medical therapy).

stem: A 70 year old lady presents to the hospital with a history of passing bright red blood mixed with stool for 3 weeks. Review of systems reveals low appetite, constipation and approximately 4kg weight loss in 2 months. She denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and fever, but she feels lethargic. On examination, she is pale. Vital signs: BP: 110/70, pulse 92/min and temperature: 37, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly patient, rectal bleeding mixed with stool, change in bowel habit, weight loss and anemia → colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.

why.C: Diverticulitis presents with LLQ pain and fever.
why.D: IBD usually presents younger with diarrhea.

stem: A 62 year old man presented to the outpatient department complaining of hematochezia for 3 months. Physical examination revealed third degree hemorrhoids. Which of the following is an appropriate initial step in management?
srcNote: He is over 45 so we need to do colonoscopy.
expl: Hematochezia in a 62-year-old must be investigated with colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer, even if hemorrhoids are found.

why.A: Treating before excluding cancer is wrong.
why.C: Same.

stem: A 30 year-old male has bloody diarrhea, 10-15 episodes a day for 6 months. Come to you in the ER. He is dehydrated, sick and cachectic. What will you do?

opts.t: Admit, monitor and give I.V fluids.
Discharge and follow up at clinic

expl: Chronic severe bloody diarrhoea, now dehydrated and sick → admit, monitor and give IV fluids (likely acute severe colitis); then steroids and investigations.

why.C: Antidiarrhoeals risk toxic megacolon in colitis.

stem: What is the most useful imaging modality to localize the site of bleeding in a patient with active lower GI bleed?
srcNote: (Gastrointestinal bleeding retroperitoneum) Active bleed or Unstable requires CT angiography while inactive bleed or stable requires colonoscopy
expl: Active lower GI bleeding → CT angiography localizes the bleeding point (≥ 0.3–0.5 mL/min) and guides embolization.

why.A: Colonoscopy is hard during massive bleeding.
why.C: Plain CT doesn't show extravasation.
why.D: Double-contrast CT is not for active bleeding.

stem: A 72-year-old diabetic man presented to the ER complaining of lower abdominal pain, nausea and bloody diarrhea for 2 days. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Blood pressure 110/65 mmHg Heart rate 85 /min Temperature 38.2 Respiratory rate 18/min Test Result Normal value WBC 17.4 4-10.5 x 10 9 L Plain abdominal x-ray: thickened descending and sigmoid colon with thumb printing appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly diabetic, LLQ pain, bloody diarrhoea, leukocytosis, and thumb-printing (submucosal oedema/haemorrhage) of the descending/sigmoid colon (watershed) → ischaemic colitis.

why.A: Diverticulitis gives LLQ pain and fever but not bloody diarrhoea with thumb-printing.
why.B: UC starts in the rectum in younger patients.
why.C: Correct.

stem: A 70-year-old man presented to the ER with a history of 6 episodes of passing large amount of fresh blood per-rectum for 12 hours, but no abdominal pain. On examination, he was pale, with BP of 90/55 mmHg, and HR= 105 b/m, Hemodynamic resuscitation and monitoring was initiated. Nasogastric tube was draining greenish fluids. Which of the following is the most likely source of the bleeding:
expl: Keyed: elderly, large painless fresh rectal bleeding, shocked → angiodysplasia (common in the elderly; diverticulosis is the other main cause).

why.C: UC gives bloody diarrhoea with pain.

stem: Which of the following anatomical landmark define the upper from the lower GI bleeding?
srcNote: , Ligament of Treitzat 4th part of duodenum
expl: Upper vs lower GI bleeding is defined by the ligament of Treitz at the duodenojejunal junction (4th part of the duodenum).

why.A: The first part of the duodenum is still upper GI.
why.C: The mid-transverse colon is the midgut/hindgut boundary, not the bleeding landmark.
why.D: The ileocaecal junction separates small from large bowel.

stem: Forgot the exact scenario, but they said they did imaging and it showed thumbprint Sign:
expl: Thumbprinting on imaging = submucosal oedema/haemorrhage of the colonic wall → ischaemic colitis (classically splenic flexure/sigmoid).

why.C: UC can thumbprint in severe cases, but the classic answer is ischaemic colitis.

stem: 70 years old woman complains of several hours of painless massive rectal bleeding. Nasogastric aspirate shows bile but no blood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Painless massive rectal bleeding in an elderly patient with an NG aspirate containing bile and no blood (upper source excluded) → diverticular bleeding.

why.A: Infective colitis gives diarrhoea and pain.
why.C: Ischaemic colitis gives pain then bloody diarrhoea.

stem: A 27 y/o man presents to the emergency department with painful rectal bleeding. He mentioned that the pain is most severe during and immediately after defecating blood red. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
srcNote: anal fissure is the only painful option in this scenario
expl: Painful bright red bleeding, worst during and after defecation = anal fissure (tear in the sensitive anoderm). Internal haemorrhoids are painless.

why.C: External haemorrhoids hurt when thrombosed, not with every defecation.
why.D: Tumours usually bleed painlessly with a change in bowel habit.

stem: A 35 YO female diagnosed as a case of (angiodysplasia) was hemodynamically unstable with massive per rectal bleeding. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in management?
srcNote: Source key was B; corrected — see explanation. (Lower GI bleeding) Source note (428 Q18 (p. 303)): Answer: A (Lower GI bleeding) Note: if the patient was stable the management will be different ( therapeutic colonoscopy ) Source note (427 F Q8 (p. 307)): Answer: A, (Lower GI bleeding) hemodynamically unstable patient - In an unstable patient with active bleeding intravenous fluid resuscitation should be started immediately. If the patient is obtunded with a thready pulse, hypoxic, having active hematemesis, and unable to protect the airway, then they need to be intubated and admitted in the intensive care unit for frequent CBC monitoring and blood transfusion as required. An endoscopy or colonoscopy should be done if possible, but it may not be possible if the patient is actively bleeding. In that case, surgery or radiology intervention with angiography is usually required
expl: Two of the three source versions keyed angiographic embolization, and it matches the doctor's algorithm: unstable bleeding from a known lesion → resuscitate → localise → angiographic embolization; surgery if that fails or isn't available. (One version keyed immediate surgery.)

why.B: Surgery if embolization fails or the bleed can't be localised.
why.C: Endoscopy is difficult during massive bleeding; endoscopic therapy is for stable patients.

stem: A 35 year old male attended the out-patient clinic with a history of recurrent attacks of bleeding per-rectum and pain during defecation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of bleeding?
expl: Recurrent bleeding with pain on defecation → anal fissure.

why.C: IBD gives diarrhoea and mucus.

stem: A 70 YO male presented to the emergency department with massive bleeding per-rectum. He was tachycardic and hypotensive. His hemoglobin on arrival was 6.0 g/dl. which of the following is the most likely cause of this massive bleeding?
expl: Keyed: massive bleeding in an elderly man with shock → angiodysplasia (with diverticulosis, the commonest causes of massive LGIB in the elderly).

why.A: A fissure causes small painful bleeds.
why.C: FAP is younger and bleeds less dramatically.

stem: An old man presented with bleeding with diarrhea for a couple of days and left iliac fossa pain and tenderness and AXR shows thick sigmoid mucosa , what’s your management ?

opts.t: do chest x-ray to rule out perforation.

srcNote: Approach to the Sick Surgical Patient / Critical Care
expl: Elderly with bloody diarrhoea, LIF pain and a thick sigmoid wall → colitis (ischaemic or diverticular inflammation) → supportive care: IV fluids and antibiotics, NPO.

why.B: Steroids could be harmful if infective/ischaemic.
why.C: Colonoscopy is risky acutely.
why.D: There is no sign of perforation.

stem: A male patient presented with recurrent fistula, bloody mucus stool and tenesmus, colonoscopy showed unhealthy rectum, what is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The source accepted both: recurrent fistulae and an unhealthy rectum suggest Crohn's (fistulizing perianal disease), while bloody mucus and tenesmus with rectal involvement suggest UC.

why.C: IBS doesn't cause fistulae or bleeding.

stem: 35 y/o, 6 times bloody, fever, leukocytosis, generalized abdominal tenderness, next step in management is:
expl: Keyed: severe/fulminant colitis (6 bloody stools, fever, leukocytosis) with generalized tenderness (peritonism — possible perforation/toxic colitis) → emergency colectomy. Without peritonism, IV steroids would come first.

why.B: First-line for acute severe UC without peritonitis.
why.C: Colonoscopy risks perforation in severe colitis.

stem: Patient with massive bleeding per rectum, diagnosed to have angiodysplasia, hemodynamically unstable, next step in Tx:
srcNote: , hemodynamically unstable patient - In an unstable patient with active bleeding intravenous fluid resuscitation should be started immediately. If the patient is obtunded with a thready pulse, hypoxic, having active hematemesis, and unable to protect the airway, then they need to be intubated and admitted in the intensive care unit for frequent CBC monitoring and blood transfusion as required. An endoscopy or colonoscopy should be done if possible, but it may not be possible if the patient is actively bleeding. In that case, surgery or radiology intervention with angiography is usually required
expl: Massive bleeding from angiodysplasia in an unstable patient → resuscitation then angiographic embolization (localises and treats); surgery if it fails.

why.C: Endoscopic cautery is for stable patients.
why.D: Sclerotherapy is not used for angiodysplasia.

stem: 70 years old lady presented to ER with 2 days Hx of rectal bleeding. Her vital signs were stable. She had similar attacks in the past with no Hx of abdominal pain. On Ex, no abdominal tenderness with positive rectal bleeding. Her dx:
srcNote: ??, probably diverticulosis cause of painless bleeding + Age of pt.
expl: Elderly woman with recurrent painless rectal bleeding and a soft abdomen → diverticulosis (bleeding).

why.A: Polyps bleed less and rarely recur this way.
why.C: Diverticulitis causes pain/fever, not typically bleeding.

stem: Same lady in Q18, a few hours later, she collapsed with increase in HR and systolic blood pressure of 80 despite blood transfusion. best next management?

opts.t: RBC scan to localize the site of bleeding

expl: Keyed: persistent bleeding with shock despite transfusion → transfusion + laparotomy + total (subtotal) colectomy, because the bleeding diverticulum hasn't been localised. (Today, CT angiography/embolization would come first if she can be stabilised.)

why.B: RBC scan is too slow in an unstable patient.
why.C: Right hemicolectomy is a blind segmental resection — high re-bleeding risk.

stem: old male present with bleeding per rectum, Normal colonoscopy what is next step

opts.t: Small bowel study to exclude cancer
Upper GI endoscopy to exclude upper GI source

expl: Rectal bleeding with a normal colonoscopy → exclude a brisk upper GI source with upper endoscopy next (more common than small-bowel causes, which are ~5%).

why.B: Small bowel studies come after upper and lower sources are excluded.
why.C: Correct.
